History & Heritage

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Are we preserving our museums and taking care of our heritage sites? Carte Blanche investigates the funding, the management and the overall experience of several historical sites.

Unique Selling Point:
We have undercover footage that shows, and sources who say our museums are not being taken care of. We went to the Boer Concentration camp Suideroord - it was overrun with weeds and has been forgotten. Vredefort Dome in the Freestate has never even opened because the building is structurally unsafe. And the Johannesburg Art Gallery has been closed since its roof caved in, as the contractors hired were not knowledgeable in conserving the historical building. We have footage of all the empty glass displays at MuseuMAfrica, which has also had several thefts - in the geology department. National monuments like Jan Smuts' house have been forgotten and lie dusty and unkept. It seems the only places where and effort is made by the department of arts and culture and the city of Johannesburg has been places where visitors flock - like Maropeng, Constitution Hill, Mandela's house on Vilakazi street, and the apartheid museum. Ditsong manages 8 national museums - their military museum was relatively good, but to the trained eye several historical artifacts - like medals have been stolen and the military vehicles and canons are rusting. (not sure we can include). They also have several unqualified audits.

Summary:
We explore all the problems - we have taken Dimitra Minas - a 20 year old student from London with South African parents to most of these locations (In Johannesburg). She has traveled the world and seen many museums - in London, Paris, Russia, Netherlands etc and will give her fair comments on her overall experience at all the locations. As a device we will use her experiences with the help of undercover footage. We will look at factors like parking; building upkeep; helpful/knowledgeable staff or tour guides; entrance fees; exhibits working, interactive, informative?; Public feedback; hours of operation, restaurant and curio stores?; bathrooms and cleanliness; directions/signs and website information.

Further information:
We have spoken to several experts and insiders and these are the problems when looking at BOTH heritage sites and museums:
Generally they are loss makers – and globally require government subsidies. There are assumptions that when a hand over takes place from national government to provincial government that they will pay for themselves, but never happens. And the projected ticket sales verse the reality are always way out. Please give examples. Feasibility study.
According to the constitution, cultural matters is a shared mandate between local and national, and therefore local government says it’s not up to them.
There is no awareness or knowledge of how to care for museums or heritage by the new administration.
There is a perception that government doesn’t transform but no public monuments or memorials have been added – the bulk of the sites are former ex-monuments –Why aren’t you declaring more sites? Need examples. Many property owners don’t even know their status. Need examples.
Provincial government are still trying to find out what they own. For example the busts – they have no knowledge of what they have.
The national audit has been completed and there is a state asset register, but no one has access to it, and it doesn’t have dates. No details – who is responsible for this? Who can we speak to about this?
All buildings/properties are managed and owned by government, which means they need to comply with building codes.
Only a small part of the system is working in reality.
Where are the inspectors and who do they work for?
Is it public works or DAC who recommends what is approved for work? This process is often overruled and the necessary work is not done.
The piece of legislation – that the statutory bodies need to comply is not adhered to. We are investing in our heritage and so it should be funded. It’s often underfunded.
Financial management of Heritage Sites/Museums: What are we looking at in terms of funding? How much? Which departments? How is accounted for? Audits for ditsong are always qualified? More information.
Where are the asset registers since the handover in 1994? Where are the requirement plans? Where is the accounting and asset management?

Antionette Murdoch has spoken out very publicly about her time as the curator at JAG and she can explain many of the problems through her experience.
Head of conservation at the Institution for planning and assessment explains that the problem is multilayered and that there are many issues - mostly at a managerial and curator level as there is a lack of understanding of preservation and security.
James Ball and Jacques Stoltz together formed a watch group for museums and heritage sites - they have made their own lists and can add an overall picture as to what is happening to our heritage sites. Both has spoken to some of my insiders and can also tell their stories. They have extensive knowledge of the national policy issues at play and were able to assist me in finding people to speak and what to look for at the different locations.


Extra Budget Items:
Travel and investigation at all the sites

Press Release:


Heritage and History
Are we keeping South Africa’s history alive by expertly preserving the country’s heritage sites and museums? Why do some sites offer a firstworld
tourist experience while other galleries and heritage buildings are closed due to neglect? Carte Blanche investigates the funding, artefact
preservation and quality of exhibits at several historic sites

Script:


Video Audio
Asteroid hurtling towards earth GETTY/GALLO
Asteroid Two billion years ago, an asteroid the size of table mountain slammed into the earth.
Graeme Graeme: “It knocked a hole in the earth between 50 and 70km deep. It’s the holy grail of impact sites in the world.”
explosion Tour operator Graeme Addison says the massive explosion formed hills that run from Parys to Johannesburg.
Graeme Graeme: “The Vredefort dome is the world’s oldest and largest visible asteroid impact site, the area was declared in 2005 as a UNESCO world heritage site.”
Shots of centre August 2014 South Africa has several other world heritage sites – like Robben Island and the Cradle of Humankind. Vredefort has an interpretation centre that explains the sites significance to visitors. The building was already completed in December 2011, but has never been opened to the public.
Graeme Graeme: “This building is almost the signature of failure.”
SITE SAHRA – context
Same image…square
15 million rand Sources say the building cost 15 million rand, but it’s been deemed unsafe as its foundation is flawed and there are cracks in the walls. Vredefort is one of South Africa’s documented heritage sites, but several museums, galleries and places of heritage remain undeclared.
Bongani LINK – site visits

STRAP – constitution hill Bongani: “WE DECIDED TO CONDUCT SITE VISITS SO THAT WE COULD ESTABLISH A STANDARD BY WHICH THEY MIGHT ALL BE MEASURED, WE OBVIOUSLY WENT TO SOME OF THE GOOD ONES LIKE THESE ISOLATION CELLS AT THE OLD FORT, WHAT IS NOW CONSTITUTION HILL, WE ALSO DECIDED TO TAKE ALONG A STUDENT FROM LONDON TO GET A SENSE OF WHAT THE INTERNATIONAL COMPARISON MIGHT BE.”
Dimitra Dimitra: “The places you can learn are in museums.”
intro Dimitra Mina has visited museums around the world as she grew up in several countries from Hungary and Russia to the Netherlands and London.
Dimitra: ann frank and telling a story Dimitra: “In school, we had to read Anne Frank and then of course you go on a trip to the Anne Frank museum, and having that whole experience and ending at the museum, really gives you deeper understanding into the culture and the heritage of a country.”
Vredefort vs Maropeng

We visited 15 sites of historical significance; In comparison to the Vredefort Dome, Dimitra’s experience at Maropeng was interactive and informative.
Dimitra on maropeng, cradle of human kind Dimitra: “It was extremely educational. It blew me away, first world experience.”
Show undercover footage
Visuals of JAG
(swop shots) Our undercover footage shows the displayed artefacts were in pristine condition. Comparatively, this 115-year-old heritage building in Joubert Park was in need of preservation. It houses the Johannesburg Art Gallery or JAG.
Antoinette – ex curator JAG Antoinette: “The Johannesburg Art Gallery has work by Picasso, I think there’s about 19 Pieces.”
Intro to antoinette JAG’s curator of 7-and-a-half years, Antoinette Murdoch, says with 30,000 visitors a year, it’s the most visited gallery in Africa.
Antointette - Antoinette: “You know I love the Johannesburg art gallery, every day I walked in, and I could smell the smell of art.”
Funding was sparse.
Antoinette Antoinette: “Every year we were given the opportunity to make a budget and then towards the end of the financial year, there would be no toilet paper. I managed to raise 15 million rands to upgrade the facility, and specifically fix the roof. The roof is the biggest problem because every time it rains, we have huge floods.”
Undercover footage But the roof renovations were never completed.
Antoinette Antoinette: “While the renovations took place a lot of the copper sheeting was stolen from the building, literally folded up, put in bags and carried out.”
JAG closed (undercover) In January this year, fed up, Antoinette resigned. JAG is currently closed, because the building is unsafe. Heritage historians Jacque Stoltz and James Ball want to speak up for heritage buildings like JAG and the Fietas Museum in Fordsburg. This lead to them co-founding the Heritage Monitoring Project.
Jacques Stoltz Jacques Stoltz: “It’s about really understanding how heritage is being dealt with in a post-democratic South Africa as a tool for addressing serious issues from the past.”
James Ball James Ball: “We want to track heritage sites and sites of significance that are in danger overtime, we want to gather evidence so we can build a really strong case for preservation.”
DAC Ndima: “When it comes to maintenance of these institutions, it’s very expensive.”
DAC intro
4 billion on screen
ACTING ARTS AND CULTURE DIRECTOR
Jan smuts visuals – photos centurion Acting Arts and Culture Director-General Vusithemba Ndima says their R4 billion rand budget is too small to properly maintain our museums and heritage sites. The department is tasked with protecting our heritage nationally, but locally municipalities safeguard places of heritage like Museum Africa. When it comes to private museums like the Jan Smuts House in Irene, Centurion, funding depends on donors.
Ndima intv Ndima: “It would be a bit idealistic to think that they could totally stand on their own without any government financial injection.”
Bongani: “It’s frustrating, it’s heart-breaking in some instances… take the Johannesburg art gallery, it probably, I mean, it probably has the most extensive collection on the continent.”
Ndima: “No, I’m aware of the fact that the city has been working on that.”
CITY OF JOBURG MMC intro The new city of Johannesburg’s head of Community Development, Nonhlanhla Sifumba is auditing their 165 heritage buildings.
CITY OF JOBURG Bongani: “How bad was it when you found it?”
Nonhlanhla: “It was very bad, I had to declare a closure immediately because ppl’s lives were in danger, the ceiling may fall at any time.”
ROOF? The city promises that by May JAGs roof restoration will begin, but budgets are tight. The funding problem may lie in confusion in the heritage act; because heritage protection is a shared responsibility between the national and local governments, and this often leads to no one wanting to take charge when things go wrong.
DAC Ndima: “We haven’t established a coordination that happens at the local level of government.”
Bongani: “Are they accountable to you?”
Ndima: “They are accountable yes, there are limitations in terms of what we can do.”
Bongani: “It seems an own goal almost all the time, you’ve got these expensive buildings that are hard to maintain, and the more they’re allowed to deteriorate, the more money it’s going to cost to get them to a state of repair?
Ndima: “I do agree, but also, understand one thing, some of these buildings are very old…it’s not going to be there forever…”
Bongani: “Wow, it’s not going to be there forever, that’s our best answer to that?”
Ndima: “It’s not the best answer, but I’m just being realistic.”
Ndima also says he was unaware of Vredefort’s 15 million rand interpretation centre - which was built 5 years ago.
DAC Ndima: “I’m hearing for the first time from you, I don’t know, I’m not aware of that.”
Bongani: “You see this is the difficulty that we have, there’s a hands off approach when things go wrong, well it’s really up to local municipality, or it’s really up to the specific management? You’re not responsible?
Ndima: “We don’t have oversight on all these museums.”
Bongani: “But aren’t you the ultimate custodians of our culture and heritage? Why have a department then?”
Ndima: “We are the custodians of culture and heritage.”
Bongani: “So should you not make sure that these sites are at least being operated properly?”
Ndima: “You’re right, but of course, first and foremost we, also, must get information.”
Show sign closed At the World Famous Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum in Soweto, information was also found lacking. We visited on a Friday morning, but it was unexpectedly closed.
DAC Ndima: “It’s closed, but I’m informed. In a couple of weeks it will be opened.”
At Constitution hill the tour guides were well informed.
Subtitle + hidden camera Upsound: “And this was lit when we were celebrating the 15th anniversary of the signing of the South African constitution on the 10th of December 2011.”
exhibits Exhibits like Nelson Mandela’s isolation cell inside The Old Fort were inspiring.
Bongani LINK LINK: “YOU REMEMBER WHAT HAS HAPPENED IN THE PAST, SO THAT IN FUTURE, YOU CAN AVOID IT. THE HAUNTING WORDS OF NELSON MANDELA, AND HERE PRESERVED IN PRISTINE CONDITION ARE HIS PERSONAL ARTIFACTS; IN THAT ALMOST ICONIC HAND WRITING, DIARY ENTRY’S, ITS COVERED IN GLASS SO THAT I CAN’T EVEN TOUCH IT, WHAT A GREAT LOSS IT WOULD BE IF WE NO LONGER HAD THESE.”
Vilakazi street Nelson Mandela’s house in Soweto is a heritage site. It’s one of our biggest tourist hotspots.
Show historial things of mandela
Dimitra – mandela house Dimitra: “It was incredible, there were tours going on in many different languages, they had such a wide array of knowledge of the place.”
Museum Africa, Newtown intro

(check shots – take out sign) Jacques and James have been monitoring Museum Africa near Newtown. So we sent in Dimitra, our international student. She was disappointed with the empty geology exhibits, vacant display cases and, even, closed exhibits – like this camera obscurer.
Dimitra international student
Moving image Dimitra: “We had to ask a custodian, oh sorry, what’s in this room, and she had to go ask a custodian permission, unlock it, it actually gave you a 360 view of real time of what was going on, on this highway.”
Gems – Nationally many museums lack basic security or even a proper staff compliment. Government says despite the lack of funding and availability of skilled staff, they are working to address these issues.
James ball, heritage monitoring project James: “We often don’t know what’s been taken and what’s still there because we don’t have the resources to audit and to document.”
Ndima Bongani: “Do you have a national asset register?
Ndima: “We don’t have a national asset register, but each museum has its own register.”
Bongani: “But if we don’t have a national asset register to compare what they say they have, and what you think they should have, isn’t that an obvious gap?”
Ndima: “Well I think it is, and it’s something I fully agree with you.”
Bongani: “Given the limited resources you have, isn’t that all the more reason to take stock and know exactly what is going on?
Ndima: “We do take stock, they’re called upon to do inventories, so they can be able to manage it.”
skills Managing those inventories also involves preservation skills.
Hazel Hazel: “If you are wanting to perform conservation on a sensitive object you need skills that are based in science, chemistry, sometimes even physics, to know what the vectors of deterioration are, You need a lab where you can run trials.
South African Institute for Heritage Science Conservation. Skills we sadly lack. Preservation of exhibits and artefacts is misunderstood says preservation scientist Hazel Botha.
Hazel Botha Hazel: “It’s important to remember that conservation applies to everything from buildings, structures, sites…even the smallest Mapungubwe bead.”
Page view street
According to the heritage monitoring project many heritage buildings aren’t being declared and are therefore not preserved. The Fietas Museum in Pageview, near Fordsburg is a protected heritage building – it’s all that’s left of 14th street.
SALMA PATEL Salma: “It survived the bulldozers of the apartheid regime.”
Museum The museum’s curator Salma Patel says the building reflects the history of the forced removals of non-whites during apartheid.
SALMA PATEL Salma: “It showcases a particular aspect of South African history and some of the awful crimes against humanity.”
Bongani LINK LINK: “SOME NAMES WILL SIMPLY NEVER BE FORGOTTEN, MANDELA, GHANDI… THESE ARE TOWERING FIGURES IN OUR HISTORY, WHICH BEGS THE QUESTION, ARE SOME OF THESE MONUMENTS BEING NEGLECTED BECAUSE WHO THEY COMMEMORATE, IS A LITTLE TOO INCONVENIENT.”
jacques Jacques believes there needs to be public debate regarding how we deal with our colonial heritage - like that of the Jan Smuts house museum – which is in run privately and is in desperate need of funding for preservation and refurbishments.
Jacques: “If we don’t have proper heritage management in place, a lot of that history corrodes, it gets lost, and once it is lost, it’s lost.”
12.00
















PROMO 1: 10 SECONDS
Is our museums and heritage sites being protected, we investigate.
Graeme: “This building is almost the signature of failure.”

PROMO 2:
Are our museums and heritage site being protected? Our undercover cameras catch empty display cases, missing artefacts and buildings in needs of repair.
Bongani: “How bad was it when you found it?”
Nonhlanhla: “It was very bad, I had to declare a closure immediately.”

PROMO 3:
Are we keeping the nation’s history alive by preserving the country’s heritage sites and museums? We investigate the funding, artefact preservation and tourist experience at several historic sites.

Graeme Graeme: “This building is almost the signature of failure.” SITE SAHRA – context Same image…square 15 million rand Sources say the building cost 15 million rand, but it’s been deemed unsafe as its foundation is flawed and there are cracks in the walls. Vredefort is one of South Africa’s documented heritage sites, but several museums, galleries and places of heritage remain undeclared. Bongani LINK – site visits STRAP – constitution hill Bongani: “WE DECIDED TO CONDUCT SITE VISITS SO THAT WE COULD ESTABLISH A STANDARD BY WHICH THEY MIGHT ALL BE MEASURED, WE OBVIOUSLY WENT TO SOME OF THE GOOD ONES LIKE THESE ISOLATION CELLS AT THE OLD FORT, WHAT IS NOW CONSTITUTION HILL, WE ALSO DECIDED TO TAKE ALONG A STUDENT FROM LONDON TO GET A SENSE OF WHAT THE INTERNATIONAL COMPARISON MIGHT BE.” Dimitra Dimitra: “The places you can learn are in museums.” intro Dimitra Mina has visited museums around the world as she grew up in several countries from Hungary and Russia to the Netherlands and London. Dimitra: ann frank and telling a story Dimitra: “In school, we had to read Anne Frank and then of course you go on a trip to the Anne Frank museum, and having that whole experience and ending at the museum, really gives you deeper understanding into the culture and the heritage of a country.” Vredefort vs Maropeng We visited 15 sites of historical significance; In comparison to the Vredefort Dome, Dimitra’s experience at Maropeng was interactive and informative. Dimitra on maropeng, cradle of human kind Dimitra: “It was extremely educational. It blew me away, first world experience.” Show undercover footage Visuals of JAG (swop shots) Our undercover footage shows the displayed artefacts were in pristine condition. Comparatively, this 115-year-old heritage building in Joubert Park was in need of preservation. It houses the Johannesburg Art Gallery or JAG. Antoinette – ex curator JAG Antoinette: “The Johannesburg Art Gallery has work by Picasso, I think there’s about 19 Pieces.” Intro to antoinette JAG’s curator of 7-and-a-half years, Antoinette Murdoch, says with 30,000 visitors a year, it’s the most visited gallery in Africa. Antointette - Antoinette: “You know I love the Johannesburg art gallery, every day I walked in, and I could smell the smell of art.” Funding was sparse. Antoinette Antoinette: “Every year we were given the opportunity to make a budget and then towards the end of the financial year, there would be no toilet paper. I managed to raise 15 million rands to upgrade the facility, and specifically fix the roof. The roof is the biggest problem because every time it rains, we have huge floods.” Undercover footage But the roof renovations were never completed. Antoinette Antoinette: “While the renovations took place a lot of the copper sheeting was stolen from the building, literally folded up, put in bags and carried out.” JAG closed (undercover) In January this year, fed up, Antoinette resigned. JAG is currently closed, because the building is unsafe. Heritage historians Jacque Stoltz and James Ball want to speak up for heritage buildings like JAG and the Fietas Museum in Fordsburg. This lead to them co-founding the Heritage Monitoring Project. Jacques Stoltz Jacques Stoltz: “It’s about really understanding how heritage is being dealt with in a post-democratic South Africa as a tool for addressing serious issues from the past.” James Ball James Ball: “We want to track heritage sites and sites of significance that are in danger overtime, we want to gather evidence so we can build a really strong case for preservation.” DAC Ndima: “When it comes to maintenance of these institutions, it’s very expensive.” DAC intro 4 billion on screen ACTING ARTS AND CULTURE DIRECTOR Jan smuts visuals – photos centurion Acting Arts and Culture Director-General Vusithemba Ndima says their R4 billion rand budget is too small to properly maintain our museums and heritage sites. The department is tasked with protecting our heritage nationally, but locally municipalities safeguard places of heritage like Museum Africa. When it comes to private museums like the Jan Smuts House in Irene, Centurion, funding depends on donors. Ndima intv Ndima: “It would be a bit idealistic to think that they could totally stand on their own without any government financial injection.” Bongani: “It’s frustrating, it’s heart-breaking in some instances… take the Johannesburg art gallery, it probably, I mean, it probably has the most extensive collection on the continent.” Ndima: “No, I’m aware of the fact that the city has been working on that.” CITY OF JOBURG MMC intro The new city of Johannesburg’s head of Community Development, Nonhlanhla Sifumba is auditing their 165 heritage buildings. CITY OF JOBURG Bongani: “How bad was it when you found it?” Nonhlanhla: “It was very bad, I had to declare a closure immediately because ppl’s lives were in danger, the ceiling may fall at any time.” ROOF? The city promises that by May JAGs roof restoration will begin, but budgets are tight. The funding problem may lie in confusion in the heritage act; because heritage protection is a shared responsibility between the national and local governments, and this often leads to no one wanting to take charge when things go wrong. DAC Ndima: “We haven’t established a coordination that happens at the local level of government.” Bongani: “Are they accountable to you?” Ndima: “They are accountable yes, there are limitations in terms of what we can do.” Bongani: “It seems an own goal almost all the time, you’ve got these expensive buildings that are hard to maintain, and the more they’re allowed to deteriorate, the more money it’s going to cost to get them to a state of repair? Ndima: “I do agree, but also, understand one thing, some of these buildings are very old…it’s not going to be there forever…” Bongani: “Wow, it’s not going to be there forever, that’s our best answer to that?” Ndima: “It’s not the best answer, but I’m just being realistic.” Ndima also says he was unaware of Vredefort’s 15 million rand interpretation centre - which was built 5 years ago. DAC Ndima: “I’m hearing for the first time from you, I don’t know, I’m not aware of that.” Bongani: “You see this is the difficulty that we have, there’s a hands off approach when things go wrong, well it’s really up to local municipality, or it’s really up to the specific management? You’re not responsible? Ndima: “We don’t have oversight on all these museums.” Bongani: “But aren’t you the ultimate custodians of our culture and heritage? Why have a department then?” Ndima: “We are the custodians of culture and heritage.” Bongani: “So should you not make sure that these sites are at least being operated properly?” Ndima: “You’re right, but of course, first and foremost we, also, must get information.” Show sign closed At the World Famous Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum in Soweto, information was also found lacking. We visited on a Friday morning, but it was unexpectedly closed. DAC Ndima: “It’s closed, but I’m informed. In a couple of weeks it will be opened.” At Constitution hill the tour guides were well informed. Subtitle + hidden camera Upsound: “And this was lit when we were celebrating the 15th anniversary of the signing of the South African constitution on the 10th of December 2011.” exhibits Exhibits like Nelson Mandela’s isolation cell inside The Old Fort were inspiring. Bongani LINK LINK: “YOU REMEMBER WHAT HAS HAPPENED IN THE PAST, SO THAT IN FUTURE, YOU CAN AVOID IT. THE HAUNTING WORDS OF NELSON MANDELA, AND HERE PRESERVED IN PRISTINE CONDITION ARE HIS PERSONAL ARTIFACTS; IN THAT ALMOST ICONIC HAND WRITING, DIARY ENTRY’S, ITS COVERED IN GLASS SO THAT I CAN’T EVEN TOUCH IT, WHAT A GREAT LOSS IT WOULD BE IF WE NO LONGER HAD THESE.” Vilakazi street Nelson Mandela’s house in Soweto is a heritage site. It’s one of our biggest tourist hotspots. Show historial things of mandela Dimitra – mandela house Dimitra: “It was incredible, there were tours going on in many different languages, they had such a wide array of knowledge of the place.” Museum Africa, Newtown intro (check shots – take out sign) Jacques and James have been monitoring Museum Africa near Newtown. So we sent in Dimitra, our international student. She was disappointed with the empty geology exhibits, vacant display cases and, even, closed exhibits – like this camera obscurer. Dimitra international student Moving image Dimitra: “We had to ask a custodian, oh sorry, what’s in this room, and she had to go ask a custodian permission, unlock it, it actually gave you a 360 view of real time of what was going on, on this highway.” Gems – Nationally many museums lack basic security or even a proper staff compliment. Government says despite the lack of funding and availability of skilled staff, they are working to address these issues. James ball, heritage monitoring project James: “We often don’t know what’s been taken and what’s still there because we don’t have the resources to audit and to document.” Ndima Bongani: “Do you have a national asset register? Ndima: “We don’t have a national asset register, but each museum has its own register.” Bongani: “But if we don’t have a national asset register to compare what they say they have, and what you think they should have, isn’t that an obvious gap?” Ndima: “Well I think it is, and it’s something I fully agree with you.” Bongani: “Given the limited resources you have, isn’t that all the more reason to take stock and know exactly what is going on? Ndima: “We do take stock, they’re called upon to do inventories, so they can be able to manage it.” skills Managing those inventories also involves preservation skills. Hazel Hazel: “If you are wanting to perform conservation on a sensitive object you need skills that are based in science, chemistry, sometimes even physics, to know what the vectors of deterioration are, You need a lab where you can run trials. South African Institute for Heritage Science Conservation. Skills we sadly lack. Preservation of exhibits and artefacts is misunderstood says preservation scientist Hazel Botha. Hazel Botha Hazel: “It’s important to remember that conservation applies to everything from buildings, structures, sites…even the smallest Mapungubwe bead.” Page view street According to the heritage monitoring project many heritage buildings aren’t being declared and are therefore not preserved. The Fietas Museum in Pageview, near Fordsburg is a protected heritage building – it’s all that’s left of 14th street. SALMA PATEL Salma: “It survived the bulldozers of the apartheid regime.” Museum The museum’s curator Salma Patel says the building reflects the history of the forced removals of non-whites during apartheid. SALMA PATEL Salma: “It showcases a particular aspect of South African history and some of the awful crimes against humanity.” Bongani LINK LINK: “SOME NAMES WILL SIMPLY NEVER BE FORGOTTEN, MANDELA, GHANDI… THESE ARE TOWERING FIGURES IN OUR HISTORY, WHICH BEGS THE QUESTION, ARE SOME OF THESE MONUMENTS BEING NEGLECTED BECAUSE WHO THEY COMMEMORATE, IS A LITTLE TOO INCONVENIENT.” jacques Jacques believes there needs to be public debate regarding how we deal with our colonial heritage - like that of the Jan Smuts house museum – which is in run privately and is in desperate need of funding for preservation and refurbishments. Jacques: “If we don’t have proper heritage management in place, a lot of that history corrodes, it gets lost, and once it is lost, it’s lost.” 12.00 PROMO 1: 10 SECONDS Is our museums and heritage sites being protected, we investigate. Graeme: “This building is almost the signature of failure.” PROMO 2: Are our museums and heritage site being protected? Our undercover cameras catch empty display cases, missing artefacts and buildings in needs of repair. Bongani: “How bad was it when you found it?” Nonhlanhla: “It was very bad, I had to declare a closure immediately.” PROMO 3: Are we keeping the nation’s history alive by preserving the country’s heritage sites and museums? We investigate the funding, artefact preservation and tourist experience at several historic sites.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Are we preserving our museums and taking care of our heritage sites? Carte Blanche investigates the funding, the management and the overall experience of several historical sites.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have undercover footage that shows, and sources who say our museums are not being taken care of. We went to the Boer Concentration camp Suideroord - it was overrun with weeds and has been forgotten. Vredefort Dome in the Freestate has never even opened because the building is structurally unsafe. And the Johannesburg Art Gallery has been closed since its roof caved in, as the contractors hired were not knowledgeable in conserving the historical building. We have footage of all the empty glass displays at MuseuMAfrica, which has also had several thefts - in the geology department. National monuments like Jan Smuts' house have been forgotten and lie dusty and unkept. It seems the only places where and effort is made by the department of arts and culture and the city of Johannesburg has been places where visitors flock - like Maropeng, Constitution Hill, Mandela's house on Vilakazi street, and the apartheid museum. Ditsong manages 8 national museums - their military museum was relatively good, but to the trained eye several historical artifacts - like medals have been stolen and the military vehicles and canons are rusting. (not sure we can include). They also have several unqualified audits.
metadata.Summary: We explore all the problems - we have taken Dimitra Minas - a 20 year old student from London with South African parents to most of these locations (In Johannesburg). She has traveled the world and seen many museums - in London, Paris, Russia, Netherlands etc and will give her fair comments on her overall experience at all the locations. As a device we will use her experiences with the help of undercover footage. We will look at factors like parking; building upkeep; helpful/knowledgeable staff or tour guides; entrance fees; exhibits working, interactive, informative?; Public feedback; hours of operation, restaurant and curio stores?; bathrooms and cleanliness; directions/signs and website information.
metadata.Further information: We have spoken to several experts and insiders and these are the problems when looking at BOTH heritage sites and museums: Generally they are loss makers – and globally require government subsidies. There are assumptions that when a hand over takes place from national government to provincial government that they will pay for themselves, but never happens. And the projected ticket sales verse the reality are always way out. Please give examples. Feasibility study. According to the constitution, cultural matters is a shared mandate between local and national, and therefore local government says it’s not up to them. There is no awareness or knowledge of how to care for museums or heritage by the new administration. There is a perception that government doesn’t transform but no public monuments or memorials have been added – the bulk of the sites are former ex-monuments –Why aren’t you declaring more sites? Need examples. Many property owners don’t even know their status. Need examples. Provincial government are still trying to find out what they own. For example the busts – they have no knowledge of what they have. The national audit has been completed and there is a state asset register, but no one has access to it, and it doesn’t have dates. No details – who is responsible for this? Who can we speak to about this? All buildings/properties are managed and owned by government, which means they need to comply with building codes. Only a small part of the system is working in reality. Where are the inspectors and who do they work for? Is it public works or DAC who recommends what is approved for work? This process is often overruled and the necessary work is not done. The piece of legislation – that the statutory bodies need to comply is not adhered to. We are investing in our heritage and so it should be funded. It’s often underfunded. Financial management of Heritage Sites/Museums: What are we looking at in terms of funding? How much? Which departments? How is accounted for? Audits for ditsong are always qualified? More information. Where are the asset registers since the handover in 1994? Where are the requirement plans? Where is the accounting and asset management? Antionette Murdoch has spoken out very publicly about her time as the curator at JAG and she can explain many of the problems through her experience. Head of conservation at the Institution for planning and assessment explains that the problem is multilayered and that there are many issues - mostly at a managerial and curator level as there is a lack of understanding of preservation and security. James Ball and Jacques Stoltz together formed a watch group for museums and heritage sites - they have made their own lists and can add an overall picture as to what is happening to our heritage sites. Both has spoken to some of my insiders and can also tell their stories. They have extensive knowledge of the national policy issues at play and were able to assist me in finding people to speak and what to look for at the different locations.
